title: Learning, Systems, and the Work of Building Organizational Capability
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez argues that learning and organizational development leaders need sharper language about what it means to be capable. She separates skill (a specific task), competency (the judgement and behaviour behind strong performance) and individual capability (drawing on all of it, in context, under pressure). Organizational capability, she says, cannot live only in people: it also requires the systems, structures, norms, tools and modelled behaviours that let people apply what they learn. Her example is a coaching-culture initiative that trains fifty managers but gives them no time, structures or accountability for coaching, so the training fails to translate. The conclusion is that learning and OD should stop defining their role as delivering learning and instead ask what the organization needs to become capable of, and what must be true of people and systems for that to happen.
points: Capability is more than knowing something or performing a skill once; it is judgement applied consistently and in context.
Five excellent managers do not make an organization strong at people management if systems do not support them.
Training managers in coaching fails when they lack time, structures and accountability to use it.
Investing in durable skills such as critical thinking, communication and situational leadership outlasts software-specific training.
The right question for learning and OD is what the organization needs to be capable of, not what training to deliver.
quotes: Individual capability, however, is different in that it looks at the entire picture. Individual capability encompasses the ability to draw on an array of knowledge, skills, behaviors, mindsets, judgments, and experiences, and use them thoughtfully and contextually when a situation calls for it.

The key here is that an individual is not a static list of attributes. They aren’t just credentials, competencies, or certifications. True capability cannot be captured on a resume or checked off in a training module; rather, it is a living, breathing asset that belongs to people.

There is also something here about choosing to invest in the skills that are, in essence, timeless, and will matter regardless of which direction we move in. Organizations that invest in capability-building are looking at the workforce skills that we’ve historically called “soft.” For these organizations, things like critical thinking, technological acumen, communication, and situational leadership matter significantly, because their shelf-life is considerably longer than a skill anchored around a software that may be obsolete in two years time.
An organization’s capability can’t live exclusively inside individual people. Many organizations think it can, and so they over-index on the development of those individuals.

The organization invests in a training program to teach 50 managers how to adopt a modern coaching approach with their direct reports. They now possess the individual skill and competency. However, those same managers return to their everyday workflows and realize they have minimal time to coach, lack the formal structures for doing it, and are never held accountable for developing their people.

The moral of the story here is recognizing that you can have individual talent, but in the absence of the right systems, how far does that really get you? True organizational capability is achieved—and sustained—only when an individual’s readiness is met with an infrastructure designed to help everyone succeed.

And perhaps this is where we need to get more precise about the work of learning and OD. Our job isn’t simply to make people better at things right now, but to help organizations become more capable of doing the things the future requires of them.
